progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b03: insulin from beta cells in the pancreatic islets; insulin binds receptors on muscle and fat cells and moves glucose transporters into the membrane; the liver stores glycogen; the usual fasting range of about 4 to 6 mmol/L; negative feedback. From b06: nutrition is an acquired cause of non-infectious disease. From b07: exposure, risk not certainty, and the artery plaque. From Year 11: red blood cells carry oxygen; enzymes; the gut absorbs nutrients; the thyroid and pituitary are endocrine glands (b01 named the pituitary). Not assumed: deficiency, excess (as defined terms), haemoglobin's iron, anaemia, collagen, scurvy, rickets, goitre, TSH, insulin resistance, risk factor, LDL.
progression.startsWith: A century ago, Australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. Today, the nutrition-linked diseases that fill our hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. One set comes from too little. The other is linked to long-term excess, alongside other risk factors. So how does what we eat change disease risk?
progression.stopsAfter: using the chain nutrient, normal job, change, effect; distinguishing deficiency (too little for long enough that a process fails) from excess (too much over years, overloading a system); explaining iron-deficiency anaemia (less haemoglobin, less oxygen carried, fatigue on exercise); explaining scurvy (vitamin C needed to build strong collagen; weak collagen, leaky vessels, bleeding gums, slow healing) and rickets (vitamin D needed to absorb calcium; soft bones bend); explaining goitre (too little iodine, less thyroid hormone, more TSH by negative feedback, the gland grows but still lacks iodine); explaining insulin resistance (excess energy and low activity build up body fat; insulin binds but fewer transporters move; glucose stays in the blood), beta cell compensation and its failure, and vessel damage from years of high glucose; distinguishing a risk factor from a certain outcome, comparing scurvy (one missing nutrient) with type 2 diabetes and heart disease (several risk factors); applying the chain to an unseen vitamin D case and evaluating a causal claim from rate data.
progression.nextLesson: when cell division escapes control: how cancer begins and spreads (bio-m8-b09). Managing type 2 diabetes: bio-m8-b12.

teaching.task: A century ago, Australian children were treated for rickets and scurvy; today the nutrition-linked diseases that fill hospitals are mostly type 2 diabetes and heart disease. How does what we eat change disease risk?
teaching.causalExplanation: Earlier, you saw that nutrition is one acquired cause of disease. Here's the chain that explains any case. Start with the nutrient and its normal job in the body. Then ask what changes when there's too little for long enough, a deficiency, or too much over many years, an excess. Then link that change to the effect. A deficiency takes away a job. An excess overloads a system that normally works. Take iron. You've seen its chain already: too little iron means less haemoglobin, smaller, paler red cells, and less oxygen carried, which is iron-deficiency anaemia. The nutrition question is why the iron is low. A diet with too little iron, or a gut that absorbs it poorly, makes it a nutritional deficiency. But losing blood, for example from heavy periods or bleeding in the gut, drains iron too, and that cause isn't the diet. So check where the iron went before you call it nutritional. The same chain works for vitamins. Vitamin C is needed by the enzymes that build strong collagen, the rope-like protein that holds together gums, skin and blood vessel walls. Without it, new collagen is weak, so small vessels leak, gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. That's scurvy. Vitamin D lets your gut absorb calcium. Without it, growing bones don't harden properly, so they can bend under the body's weight. That's rickets. Scurvy has a C in it, for vitamin C. Rickets, think vitamin D. Your skin can make it in sunlight, and some foods and supplements supply it too.
teaching.conversationalApproach: A century ago, Australian doctors still treated children for rickets, where growing bones soften and bend, and scurvy, where gums bleed and wounds won't heal. Earlier, you saw that nutrition is one acquired cause of disease. Take iron. The same chain works for vitamins. Iodine adds a twist you'll recognise from homeostasis. Now excess, and type 2 diabetes. At first, the beta cells in the pancreas cover for it by releasing more insulin, so blood glucose can stay close to normal for years. So does eating too much cause type 2 diabetes? Not on its own. Two exam questions. The nutrient is vitamin D, and its job is helping the gut absorb calcium. Second. Obesity and a family history both go with higher rates, and together, the highest. So for any nutrition question, name the nutrient and its normal job, say what changes with too little or too much, link it to the effect, then ask: is this one missing nutrient, or one risk factor among many? Next, what happens when cell division escapes control: how cancer begins and spreads.

The other is linked to long-term excess, alongside other risk factors. So how does what we eat change disease risk?
teaching.understandingCheck: Two exam questions. First. A fourteen-year-old spends almost all daylight hours indoors. Blood tests show low vitamin D, and their gut is absorbing little calcium. Using nutrient, change and effect, explain how this deficiency could affect their bones. Pause here to answer. Second. The chart shows new cases of type 2 diabetes per thousand adults each year, in four groups sorted by body weight and family history. Identify two risk factors the data show. Then explain why the claim "eating too much causes type 2 diabetes" overstates the evidence. Pause here to answer.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ2-01 (p 57): "investigate the causes and effects of non-infectious diseases in humans, including but not limited to:" with the listed example "nutritional diseases". Causes: scenes 2 to 6. Effects: scenes 3 to 5 and 7 (anaemia, scurvy, rickets, goitre, type 2 diabetes and vessel damage). Inquiry question: "Do non-infectious diseases cause more deaths than infectious diseases?" (not answered here).

design.visualSystem: One nutrient chain owns the bottom fifth of the frame from scene 2 to scene 7: four coded boxes "nutrient → normal job → change → effect" (b07's PathwayStrip with four slots), each filling with a thumbnail and two to four words for the current nutrient, with a small coded balance beam at its left end that tips to "too little" (deficiency) or "too much" (excess). Above the chain, one painted plate or matched pair at a time with callouts. In scenes 6 and 7, a small coded years strip (a horizontal 0 to 15 years axis with two rising and falling bars, "insulin" and "blood glucose") sits at the upper right. No people, hands or faces: no faces with goitres, no children's legs, no gums in a mouth; each disease is shown at organ or tissue level (bones only, thyroid only, tissue around a capillary). Coded elements are limited to the chain, the beam, the years strip, the attempt chart, glucose hexagons (b03's GlucoseDots), oxygen dots, chips, tags and arrows. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
